title: Καρύα
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 152. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Καρύα, παρά τινα ὁδὸν οὖσα καὶ ὑπὸ τῶν παριόντων λίθοις βαλλομένη, στενάξασα πρὸς ἑαυτὴν εἶπεν· « Ἀθλία εἰμὶ ἐγώ, ἥτις κατ’ ἐνιαυτὸν ἐμαυτῇ ὕβρεις καὶ λύπας παρέχω. »
sentences.tr: Karya, para tina hodon ousa kai hypo tōn pariontōn lithois ballomenē, stenaxasa pros heautēn eipen· « Athlia eimi egō, hētis kat’ eniauton emautēi hybreis kai lypas parechō. »
sentences.l: A nut tree, being beside a certain road and being pelted with stones by those passing by, having groaned, said to herself: « Wretched am I, seeing that year by year I procure for myself outrages and griefs. »
sentences.i: A nut tree that stood beside a road and was pelted with stones by passers-by groaned and said to herself: « Wretched am I, who year by year bring outrage and grief upon myself. »
sentences.n: καρύα is the nut-tree in general; the Greek names no species. ὑπό with the genitive gives the agent, λίθοις the instrument: pelted by men, with stones. The tree is feminine in Greek and speaks of herself so. ἥτις, the indefinite relative, states the ground as well as the fact, "being one who…". κατ’ ἐνιαυτόν is "year by year", the nut harvest coming round each season. ὕβρις is not mere insult but violent outrage.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος πρὸς τοὺς ἐπὶ τῶν ἰδίων ἀγαθῶν λυπουμένους.
sentences.tr: Ho logos pros tous epi tōn idiōn agathōn lypoumenous.
sentences.l: The story is directed at those who are grieved over their own good things.
sentences.i: The story is directed at those whose own advantages are the cause of their suffering.
sentences.n: The closing sentence has no verb at all: πρός with the accusative alone names the people the fable is aimed at. ἐπί with the genitive is "in the case of, over"; the dative is the commoner case after λυπέομαι for the thing grieved at. The point is precise all the same — the tree suffers not in spite of its fruit but because of it.
